content: Famotidine is a histamine H2-receptor antagonist that works by inhibiting the production of stomach acid. It is frequently used in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), also known as GORD in some regions. Famotidine is commonly marketed under the trade names Pepcidine and Pepcid by Johnson & Johnson and Merck. Certain formulations of famotidine are available over the counter (OTC) in various countries. In the United States, 10 mg and 20 mg tablets of famotidine, sometimes combined with a traditional antacid, can be purchased OTC. However, higher doses of famotidine still require a prescription. Famotidine is also administered to surgical patients prior to operations to prevent postoperative nausea and to reduce the risk of aspiration pneumonitis. Famotidine was developed by Merck & Co. and is marketed through a joint venture between Merck and Johnson & Johnson. During its development, the imidazole ring present in cimetidine was replaced with a 2-guanidinothiazole ring, resulting in famotidine being 30 times more potent than cimetidine. Famotidine was first introduced to the market in 1985. In 1999, orally disintegrating tablets of famotidine, marketed as Pepcid RPD, were released. These tablets dissolve in the mouth and do not need to be swallowed. Other brand names for famotidine include Fluxid (marketed by Schwarz) and Quamatel (marketed by Gedeon Richter Ltd.). In the United States, a product called Pepcid Complete is available, which combines famotidine with an antacid in a chewable tablet form. This formulation is designed to address the relatively slow onset of action of famotidine alone. In the United Kingdom, this product is marketed under the name Pepcidtwo.
